vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.title: Classifications of Data Structures (Primitive & Non-Primitive)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.simpleConcept: Think of data structures like kitchen containers. A single spice jar holds one item (primitive data types like int, float, char). A layered bento box or spice rack organizes multiple items together in a structured way (non-primitive data structures like arrays, stacks, and linked lists). Choosing the right container makes cooking (computing) fast and clean.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.technicalConcept:
Data structures are categorized into:
1. Primitive Data Structures: Basic types directly supported by hardware and machine instructions (int, float, char, pointer, double).
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures: Derived complex structures organizing collections of data elements.
   • Linear Data Structures: Elements form a sequential sequence (Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists). In linear structures, elements have unique predecessors and successors (except first and last).
   • Non-Linear Data Structures: Elements form hierarchical or interconnected relationships (Trees, Graphs). Each element may connect to multiple items.
keyPoints: Primitive types (int, char, float) operate directly via CPU registers and ALU instructions.
Non-primitive types organize multiple homogeneous or heterogeneous values.
Linear data structures maintain single-level sequential relationships (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues).
Non-linear structures represent hierarchical (Trees) or arbitrary network relationships (Graphs).
Primary operations include Insertion, Deletion, Traversal, Searching, Sorting, and Merging.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory Allocation in C
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.simpleConcept: A pointer is a note with a house address instead of the house itself. Dynamic memory allocation is like booking a hotel room: you don't decide how many rooms you need when building the hotel (compile-time); you ask the front desk (OS) for exactly the rooms you need when guests arrive (runtime using malloc/calloc), and you must check out (free) when you leave so memory isn't wasted.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.technicalConcept:
Pointers store memory addresses of variables. The dereference operator `*` accesses the value at that address, while address-of `&` retrieves the memory address.
Dynamic Memory Allocation (DMA) allocates heap memory at runtime via standard library `<stdlib.h>` functions:
1. `malloc(size)`: Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes; returns `void*` or NULL on failure.
2. `calloc(n, size)`: Allocates contiguous block for `n` items of `size` bytes each and initializes all bits to 0.
3. `realloc(ptr, new_size)`: Resizes previously allocated heap block, preserving existing content.
4. `free(ptr)`: Deallocates heap block to prevent memory leaks.
keyPoints: Pointer declaration `type *ptr` holds an address in virtual memory.
malloc() leaves allocated memory uninitialized with garbage values.
calloc() clears memory to zero, useful for arrays and counters.
Always check `ptr != NULL` after heap allocations to avoid segmentation faults.
Failing to call `free()` leads to memory leaks; accessing after `free()` creates dangling pointer bugs.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.title: Arrays & Dynamic Allocation Arrays
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.simpleConcept: A static array is like a locked bookshelf with 5 fixed slots built into the wall. If you buy a 6th book, you are stuck. A dynamic array is a modular shelf on wheels: you can allocate 5 slots today, and if you need more space, you order a bigger shelf, move your books over, and discard the old one.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.technicalConcept:
Arrays are contiguous blocks of homogeneous data elements accessible via zero-based indexing.
• 1D Array Address Formula: `Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + (i - LowerBound) * ElementSize`
• 2D Row-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(i * ColCount) + j] * ElementSize`
• 2D Column-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(j * RowCount) + i] * ElementSize`
Dynamic arrays overcome fixed compile-time dimensions by allocating heap pointers through `malloc/realloc`.
keyPoints: Arrays guarantee O(1) constant time random access by index.
Insertion and deletion in arbitrary positions require O(n) element shifting.
Row-major order stores elements row-by-row in linear memory (standard in C/C++).
Dynamic 2D arrays can be created via an array of pointers (`int **mat = malloc(rows * sizeof(int*))`).

examModelAnswers.question: Derive the address formula for a 2-dimensional array stored in Row-Major and Column-Major order.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
Let array A have bounds A[0...M-1][0...N-1], Base address = B, and element size = w bytes.

1. Row-Major Order:
• Elements are stored row-by-row.
• To reach element A[i][j], we must skip 'i' complete rows. Each row has 'N' elements, so `i * N` elements precede the current row.
• In row 'i', we must skip 'j' elements to reach column 'j'.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(i * N) + j] * w`.

2. Column-Major Order:
• Elements are stored column-by-column.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(j * M) + i] * w`.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.technicalConcept:
• `struct`: Composite data type where every member has its own distinct memory offset. Total size >= sum of member sizes (plus padding).

• Polynomial Representation: A polynomial P(x) = a_n x^e + ... + a_0 is represented in memory as an array of structures or linked list where each node stores `coefficient` and `exponent`.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.title: Sparse Matrix Representation (Triplet Form)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.simpleConcept: Imagine an attendance sheet with 1,000 students where only 3 students are absent. Instead of printing 1,000 names with 'Present' next to 997 of them, you just write down the 3 roll numbers who are absent. That is a sparse matrix: when most entries are zeros, we only store the non-zero values with their (row, column, value) coordinates.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.technicalConcept:
A sparse matrix is an M x N matrix in which the majority of elements are zero. Storing all elements in a standard 2D array wastes memory (O(M x N)) and CPU cycles processing zeroes.
Triplet Representation (3-Tuple Form):
An array of structures where each element has:
• `row`: Row index of non-zero value
• `col`: Column index of non-zero value
• `val`: Non-zero value
Row 0 (Header/Metadata) stores:
• `triplet[0].row = Total Rows (M)`
• `triplet[0].col = Total Columns (N)`
• `triplet[0].val = Total Non-Zero Elements (K)`
The total space occupied is (K + 1) * 3, dramatically smaller when K << M * N.
keyPoints: A matrix is sparse if zero elements significantly outnumber non-zero elements.
Standard 2D array uses O(rows * cols); Triplet form uses O(non_zeros) storage.
Row 0 is the metadata header storing matrix dimensions and total non-zero count.
Triplets are traditionally sorted by row index, then by column index.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.title: Transposing a Sparse Matrix
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.simpleConcept: Transposing means turning rows into columns (swapping i and j coordinates). If you just swap coordinates naively, the resulting triplet list won't be sorted by rows anymore! An ordinary transpose searches through all columns one by one, which is slow. Fast Transpose uses a frequency count to precalculate the exact destination slot for every element in one smooth pass.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.technicalConcept:
When transposing a sparse triplet representation, swapping `row` and `col` invalidates row-major ordering.
1. Ordinary Transpose: Iterates columns 0 to N-1; scans all K non-zero elements. Time: O(Cols * K).
2. Fast Transpose: Uses `row_terms[]` and `starting_pos[]` to place elements directly into target slots in a single pass. Time: O(Cols + K).
keyPoints: Transposing swaps (row, col) coordinates while preserving sorted row order.
Ordinary Transpose has O(cols * non_zeros) time complexity.
Fast Transpose achieves O(cols + non_zeros) using row_terms[] and starting_pos[] auxiliary arrays.
Fast Transpose requires O(cols) auxiliary memory space.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation & Stack Implementations
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.simpleConcept: A stack is like a stack of cafeteria plates: the last plate placed on top is the first one taken off (LIFO: Last-In, First-Out). You can only push a new plate onto the top or pop the top plate off. If the plate dispenser is full, pushing causes an overflow; if it's completely empty, popping causes an underflow.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.technicalConcept:
A Stack is a linear ADT restricted to LIFO (Last-In First-Out) operations occurring exclusively at one end designated as `top`.
• Primary operations:
  - `push(item)`: Increments top and stores item. Fails on Stack Overflow (`top == MAX - 1`).
  - `pop()`: Returns item at top and decrements top. Fails on Stack Underflow (`top == -1`).
  - `peek()`: Inspects top element without removing it.
• Dynamic Implementation: Allocates stack dynamically on the heap; dynamically doubles capacity via `realloc` when full, avoiding static overflow limits.
keyPoints: Stack follows LIFO discipline (Last In, First Out).
Stack Underflow occurs when pop() is attempted on an empty stack (`top == -1`).
Stack Overflow occurs in static arrays when push() is attempted and `top == MAX - 1`.
Dynamic stack uses `realloc` to double buffer size upon overflow, achieving O(1) amortized push.
Crucial in call stacks, undo/redo buffers, syntax parsing, and recursion.

2. Operations:

3. Time Complexity: Push, Pop, and Peek are all O(1) constant time operations.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion, Postfix Evaluation & Recursion
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.simpleConcept: Humans write expressions in infix notation: `A + B * C`, which requires parentheses and operator rules to know what happens first. Computers hate guessing rules: they prefer postfix (Reverse Polish) notation: `A B C * +`, where operators immediately follow their operands. Stacks convert and evaluate postfix expressions with zero ambiguity and zero parentheses!
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.technicalConcept:
1. Infix to Postfix Conversion (Shunting-Yard):
• Scan infix tokens left to right.
• If operand: output immediately to postfix string.
• If `(`: push to stack.
• If `)`: pop and output until matching `(` is encountered.
• If operator: pop operators with greater or equal precedence from stack to output, then push incoming operator.
• At end of expression: pop all remaining operators.
2. Postfix Evaluation:
• Scan postfix expression left to right.
• If operand: push value onto evaluation stack.
• If operator: pop two operands (`op2 = pop()`, `op1 = pop()`), compute `res = op1 operator op2`, push `res` back onto stack.
• Final answer is the sole value remaining on the stack.
3. Recursion & Run-Time Stack:
• Every recursive function call pushes an activation record (stack frame) storing local variables, parameters, and return address onto the system call stack.
keyPoints: Infix: `A + B`. Postfix: `A B +`. Prefix: `+ A B`.
Postfix expressions never require parentheses or precedence rules during evaluation.
Evaluation stack order is critical: `op2 = pop()`, `op1 = pop()`, then compute `op1 - op2` (not op2 - op1).
Recursion relies on the OS call stack; deep unstopped recursion causes a Stack Overflow error.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.title: Circular Queues, Double-Ended Queues & Priority Queues
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.simpleConcept: A linear queue is like a movie ticket line: people join at the back (rear) and leave from the front (front). But in a linear array queue, once people leave the front, those empty spots can never be reused without shifting everyone! A Circular Queue bends the line into a circle like a merry-go-round, wrapping around back to slot 0 so space is never wasted.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.technicalConcept:
1. Linear Queue Limitation: False Overflow occurs when `rear == MAX - 1` even though empty slots exist before `front`.
2. Circular Queue:
• Uses modulo arithmetic: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX`, `front = (front + 1) % MAX`.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
3. Deque (Double-Ended Queue): Allows insertion and deletion at both ends (`insertFront`, `deleteFront`, `insertRear`, `deleteRear`).
4. Priority Queue: Elements are served based on priority rather than arrival time (implemented using sorted arrays or heaps).
keyPoints: Linear queue suffers from false overflow due to unidirectional pointer movement.
Circular queue wraps around using modulo arithmetic: `(index + 1) % MAX`.
Deque allows operations at both ends (Input-restricted and Output-restricted variants exist).
Priority queues dequeue highest-priority items first, crucial for CPU job scheduling.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.title: Singly, Doubly & Circular Linked Lists Operations
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.simpleConcept: Think of a treasure hunt: you don't need a single big bus where everyone sits in a row (array). Each clue tells you where the next person is located across town (pointers). A Singly Linked List points only forward; a Doubly Linked List gives you clues forward and backward; a Circular Linked List loops the last clue right back to the first person!
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.technicalConcept:
A Linked List is a linear data collection composed of dynamically allocated nodes connected by pointers.
1. Singly Linked List (SLL):
• Each node has `data` and `next` pointer.
• Traversal is strictly unidirectional; inserting/deleting at head is O(1).
2. Doubly Linked List (DLL):
• Each node has `prev`, `data`, and `next` pointers.
• Supports bidirectional traversal and O(1) node deletion given node reference, at the cost of extra pointer overhead.
3. Circular Linked List (CLL):
• The `next` pointer of the last node points back to the `head` node rather than NULL, eliminating null-pointer checks during cyclic traversal.
keyPoints: Linked lists eliminate fixed capacity constraints and expensive array shifting.
SLL node has 1 pointer (`next`); DLL node has 2 pointers (`prev` and `next`).
Inserting at head: `newNode->next = head; head = newNode;` (O(1)).
Deleting a node in DLL: `node->prev->next = node->next; node->next->prev = node->prev; free(node);`
Circular lists are ideal for round-robin CPU scheduling and playlist repeat loops.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.title: Binary Trees, BST Traversals (Inorder, Preorder, Postorder)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: A family tree starts with a single ancestor (root) branching out into children. In a Binary Search Tree (BST), there is a strict rule: smaller children go to the LEFT branch, and bigger children go to the RIGHT branch. Because of this rule, reading the tree 'Inorder' (Left, Root, Right) automatically prints all numbers in perfectly sorted ascending order!
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
1. Binary Tree: A non-linear hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children (`left` and `right`).
2. Binary Search Tree (BST) Property: For every node X:
• All values in `left_subtree(X) < value(X)`
• All values in `right_subtree(X) > value(X)`
3. Tree Traversals:
• Inorder (L-D-R): Traverse left subtree, visit root, traverse right subtree. Produces sorted order in BST.
• Preorder (D-L-R): Visit root, traverse left, traverse right. Used to serialize/clone trees.
• Postorder (L-R-D): Traverse left, traverse right, visit root. Used for bottom-up cleanup (deleting trees) and postfix expressions.
keyPoints: A binary tree node contains data and two child pointers (`left` and `right`).
Inorder traversal of any valid BST yields elements in strictly sorted order.
Average time complexity for search/insert/delete in BST is O(log n); worst case is O(n) for skewed trees.
Height of a balanced tree with N nodes is ceil(log2(N + 1)).

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.title: Threaded Binary Trees & AVL Tree Rotations
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.simpleConcept: In a standard binary tree, almost half of all child pointers are NULL (wasted space!). A Threaded Binary Tree replaces those useless NULL pointers with 'threads' pointing to in-order predecessors and successors, allowing you to walk through the tree without recursion or a stack. An AVL Tree is a self-balancing gymnast: whenever one side gets too heavy, it performs rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL) to stay balanced.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.technicalConcept:
1. Threaded Binary Tree (TBT):
• Utilizes empty NULL leaf pointers to store in-order traversal pointers.
• `rthread = 1` indicates `right` points to Inorder successor; `lthread = 1` indicates `left` points to Inorder predecessor.
• Enables stackless, non-recursive Inorder traversal.
2. AVL Trees (Adelson-Velsky and Landis):
• Self-balancing BST where Balance Factor for every node is $BF = \text{height}(left) - \text{height}(right) \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$.
• When $|BF| > 1$, four rotation schemes restore balance:
  - LL Rotation: Single Right rotation on root
  - RR Rotation: Single Left rotation on root
  - LR Rotation: Left rotation on child, then Right rotation on root
  - RL Rotation: Right rotation on child, then Left rotation on root
• Guarantees strictly $O(\log n)$ worst-case search, insertion, and deletion.
keyPoints: In an N-node binary tree, exactly N + 1 pointers are NULL; TBTs repurpose them as threads.
TBT allows traversal without recursion or explicit runtime stacks.
AVL tree balance factor: BF = Height(Left) - Height(Right); must remain in {-1, 0, 1}.
LL and RR require single rotations; LR and RL require double rotations.
AVL trees strictly maintain O(log n) height, preventing O(n) degenerate skewing.

• RR Rotation (Right-Right): Inserted into right subtree of right child. BF becomes -2. Fixed by single Left Rotation on root.
• LR Rotation (Left-Right): Inserted into right subtree of left child. Fixed by double rotation: Left rotate child, then Right rotate root.
• RL Rotation (Right-Left): Inserted into left subtree of right child. Fixed by double rotation: Right rotate child, then Left rotate root.

3. Time Complexity: Rotation costs O(1); tree height is O(log n).

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.title: Binary Heaps (Max-Heap, Min-Heap) & Priority Queue Design
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.simpleConcept: Think of an emergency hospital triage: patients aren't treated in the order they arrived; the most critically ill patient gets treated first (Priority Queue). A Binary Heap is a complete tree packed into a simple flat array where the biggest (Max-Heap) or smallest (Min-Heap) element always sits at the very top (index 1), ready to be served instantly in O(1) time!
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.technicalConcept:
A Binary Heap is a Complete Binary Tree stored compactly in a contiguous array without pointers:
• Array Mapping: For element at index `i`:
  - Left Child: `2 * i`
  - Right Child: `2 * i + 1`
  - Parent: `floor(i / 2)`
• Heap Property:
  - Max-Heap: `key(parent) >= key(child)` for all nodes. Root holds maximum element.
  - Min-Heap: `key(parent) <= key(child)` for all nodes. Root holds minimum element.
• Core Operations:
  - `insert(val)`: Place at next available array slot and sift-up (Heapify-up) in $O(\log n)$.
  - `extractMax()`: Swap root with last element, decrement size, sift-down (Heapify-down) in $O(\log n)$.
  - `buildHeap`: Bottom-up heap construction runs in linear $O(n)$ time.
keyPoints: Binary Heap is a Complete Binary Tree, ensuring zero wasted slots in array representation.
Children of index i are at 2*i and 2*i + 1; parent is at floor(i/2).
Max-Heap root stores maximum; Min-Heap root stores minimum in O(1) lookup.
Insertion and extraction run in O(log n) time.
Building a heap of n elements using bottom-up heapify takes O(n) time.

examModelAnswers.question: What is a Binary Heap? Explain Max-Heap construction with an example. Write the algorithm for deleteMax().
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
A Binary Heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property. In a Max-Heap, every parent node is greater than or equal to its children.

2. Array Representation:
Elements stored from index 1 to N. Left child = 2i, Right child = 2i + 1, Parent = i/2.

3. DeleteMax Algorithm (Extract-Max):
1. Check if heap is empty (size == 0).
2. Max element is at root: `maxVal = heap[1]`.
3. Move the last leaf element to root: `heap[1] = heap[size]; size = size - 1`.
4. Call `maxHeapify(heap, 1)`: compare root with left and right children; swap with the larger child. Repeat downward until heap property is restored.
5. Return `maxVal`.

4. Complexity: Height of heap is log2(N); extraction runs in O(log n) time.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.title: Graph Representation & Traversals (BFS and DFS)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.simpleConcept: Think of a subway network or airline route map: cities are stations (vertices) and routes connecting them are tracks (edges). Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores outward in concentric ripples like waves in a pond using a Queue (closest stations first). Depth-First Search (DFS) explores one deep tunnel all the way to a dead end before backtracking using a Stack or Recursion.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.technicalConcept:
A Graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of vertices $V$ and edges $E$.
1. Representations:
• Adjacency Matrix: $V \times V$ 2D array where `matrix[u][v] = 1` if edge exists. Space: $O(V^2)$, optimal for dense graphs.
• Adjacency List: Array of linked lists where list `u` contains all neighbors of vertex `u`. Space: $O(V + E)$, optimal for sparse graphs.
2. Graph Traversals:
• Breadth-First Search (BFS):
  - Uses a FIFO Queue.
  - Explores all neighbors at current distance before moving deeper.
  - Time: $O(V + E)$. Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.
• Depth-First Search (DFS):
  - Uses LIFO Stack / Recursion.
  - Traverses as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.
  - Time: $O(V + E)$. Used for cycle detection and topological sorting.
keyPoints: Adjacency Matrix uses O(V^2) space; Adjacency List uses O(V + E) space.
BFS uses a Queue and visits vertices level-by-level (radiating outwards).
DFS uses a Stack / recursion and explores paths to dead ends before backtracking.
Both BFS and DFS maintain a `visited[]` boolean array to prevent infinite cycles.
Traversing an entire graph with BFS or DFS takes O(V + E) using adjacency lists.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.title: Hash Functions & Collision Resolution Techniques
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.simpleConcept: Think of an apartment building with mailboxes numbered 0 to 99. A hash function takes your name and calculates which mailbox slot your letter belongs to in one second (O(1)). But what if two people get assigned the exact same mailbox? That is a Collision! We resolve it either by chaining (hanging a bag underneath the mailbox) or linear probing (placing it into the next available open mailbox).
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.technicalConcept:
Hashing maps a large key space to a compact hash table index using a Hash Function $h(k)$.
1. Common Hash Functions:
• Division Method: $h(k) = k \pmod m$ (where $m$ is usually a prime number).
• Multiplication Method: $h(k) = \lfloor m (k A \pmod 1) \rfloor$.
• Mid-Square Method: Square the key and extract middle digits.
2. Collision Resolution Techniques:
• Open Hashing (Separate Chaining):
  - Each hash table slot is the head of a linked list storing all colliding keys.
  - Table never fills up; degrades gracefully as load factor $\alpha = n/m$ increases.
• Closed Hashing (Open Addressing):
  - All keys stored directly in table slots.
  - Linear Probing: $h(k, i) = (h(k) + i) \pmod m$. Suffers from primary clustering.
  - Quadratic Probing: $h(k, i) = (h(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) \pmod m$. Reduces clustering.
  - Double Hashing: $h(k, i) = (h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \pmod m$. Optimal dispersion.
keyPoints: Hashing achieves O(1) average-case search, insertion, and deletion.
A collision occurs when two distinct keys yield identical hash addresses: h(k1) == h(k2).
Separate Chaining handles collisions using linked lists attached to each bucket.
Linear Probing checks consecutive slots, causing primary clustering clusters of filled slots.
Load factor alpha = n / m measures table saturation.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.title: Merge Sort, Quick Sort & Radix Sort Complexity Analysis
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.simpleConcept: Sorting organizes messy books by title. Merge Sort is like a wise librarian who divides a giant stack into two equal halves, sorts each half, and merges them smoothly (guaranteed fast). Quick Sort picks a leader ('pivot') and tosses smaller books to the left and bigger books to the right. Radix Sort doesn't compare books at all: it sorts numbers digit by digit like postal mail sorting machines!
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.technicalConcept:
1. Merge Sort:
• Divide-and-Conquer paradigm.
• Divides array into halves, recursively sorts, and merges two sorted halves in $O(n)$ time.
• Recurrence: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) \implies O(n \log n)$ across all cases (best, average, worst).
• Stable sort, but requires $O(n)$ auxiliary space.
2. Quick Sort:
• Selects pivot element, partitions array into elements $\le$ pivot and $>$ pivot.
• Average Case: $O(n \log n)$. Worst Case: $O(n^2)$ when array is already sorted and pivot is extreme.
• In-place sort requiring $O(\log n)$ stack space.
3. Radix Sort:
• Non-comparative integer sorting algorithm.
• Processes digits from Least Significant Digit (LSD) to MSD using stable Counting Sort subroutines.
• Time Complexity: $O(d \cdot (n + k))$ where $d$ is maximum digits, $k$ is base/radix (10 for decimal).
keyPoints: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases, but requires O(n) auxiliary memory.
Quick Sort has O(n log n) average time and O(n^2) worst case, but operates in-place.
Quick Sort worst case is mitigated by randomized or median-of-three pivot selection.
Radix Sort is non-comparative, beating the O(n log n) comparison barrier with O(d * (n + k)).
Merge Sort and Radix Sort are Stable; standard Quick Sort is Unstable.

3. Swap pivot into its correct sorted position `j`.
4. Recursively call `quickSort(arr, low, j - 1)` and `quickSort(arr, j + 1, high)`.

2. Partition Trace of [26, 5, 37, 1, 61, 11, 59, 15]:
• Pivot = 26.
• Left scans forward for element > 26 (finds 37).
• Right scans backward for element < 26 (finds 15).
• Swap 37 and 15 -> [26, 5, 15, 1, 61, 11, 59, 37].
• Continue: swap 61 and 11 -> [26, 5, 15, 1, 11, 61, 59, 37].
• Pointers cross at index 4 (value 11). Swap pivot 26 with 11:
• Partitioned array: [11, 5, 15, 1] 26 [61, 59, 37]. Pivot 26 is placed.

3. Worst-Case Complexity Analysis:
Occurs when array is already sorted or reverse sorted and extreme element is always chosen as pivot.
Recurrence: T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(n) = O(n^2). Avoided via randomized or median-of-three pivot.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.title: Classifications of Data Structures (Primitive & Non-Primitive)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.simpleConcept: Think of data structures like kitchen containers. A single spice jar holds one item (primitive data types like int, float, char). A layered bento box or spice rack organizes multiple items together in a structured way (non-primitive data structures like arrays, stacks, and linked lists). Choosing the right container makes cooking (computing) fast and clean.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.technicalConcept:
Data structures are categorized into:
1. Primitive Data Structures: Basic types directly supported by hardware and machine instructions (int, float, char, pointer, double).
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures: Derived complex structures organizing collections of data elements.
   • Linear Data Structures: Elements form a sequential sequence (Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists). In linear structures, elements have unique predecessors and successors (except first and last).
   • Non-Linear Data Structures: Elements form hierarchical or interconnected relationships (Trees, Graphs). Each element may connect to multiple items.
keyPoints: Primitive types (int, char, float) operate directly via CPU registers and ALU instructions.
Non-primitive types organize multiple homogeneous or heterogeneous values.
Linear data structures maintain single-level sequential relationships (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues).
Non-linear structures represent hierarchical (Trees) or arbitrary network relationships (Graphs).
Primary operations include Insertion, Deletion, Traversal, Searching, Sorting, and Merging.

examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory Allocation in C
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.simpleConcept: A pointer is a note with a house address instead of the house itself. Dynamic memory allocation is like booking a hotel room: you don't decide how many rooms you need when building the hotel (compile-time); you ask the front desk (OS) for exactly the rooms you need when guests arrive (runtime using malloc/calloc), and you must check out (free) when you leave so memory isn't wasted.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.technicalConcept:
Pointers store memory addresses of variables. The dereference operator `*` accesses the value at that address, while address-of `&` retrieves the memory address.
Dynamic Memory Allocation (DMA) allocates heap memory at runtime via standard library `<stdlib.h>` functions:
1. `malloc(size)`: Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes; returns `void*` or NULL on failure.
2. `calloc(n, size)`: Allocates contiguous block for `n` items of `size` bytes each and initializes all bits to 0.
3. `realloc(ptr, new_size)`: Resizes previously allocated heap block, preserving existing content.
4. `free(ptr)`: Deallocates heap block to prevent memory leaks.
keyPoints: Pointer declaration `type *ptr` holds an address in virtual memory.
malloc() leaves allocated memory uninitialized with garbage values.
calloc() clears memory to zero, useful for arrays and counters.
Always check `ptr != NULL` after heap allocations to avoid segmentation faults.
Failing to call `free()` leads to memory leaks; accessing after `free()` creates dangling pointer bugs.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.simpleConcept: A static array is like a locked bookshelf with 5 fixed slots built into the wall. If you buy a 6th book, you are stuck. vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.technicalConcept:
Arrays are contiguous blocks of homogeneous data elements accessible via zero-based indexing.
• 1D Array Address Formula: `Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + (i - LowerBound) * ElementSize`
• 2D Row-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(i * ColCount) + j] * ElementSize`
• 2D Column-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(j * RowCount) + i] * ElementSize`
Dynamic arrays overcome fixed compile-time dimensions by allocating heap pointers through `malloc/realloc`.
keyPoints: Arrays guarantee O(1) constant time random access by index.
Insertion and deletion in arbitrary positions require O(n) element shifting.
Row-major order stores elements row-by-row in linear memory (standard in C/C++).
Dynamic 2D arrays can be created via an array of pointers (`int **mat = malloc(rows * sizeof(int*))`).

Let array A have bounds A[0...M-1][0...N-1], Base address = B, and element size = w bytes.

2. Column-Major Order:
• Elements are stored column-by-column.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(j * M) + i] * w`.

• Polynomial Representation: A polynomial P(x) = a_n x^e + ... + a_0 is represented in memory as an array of structures or linked list where each node stores `coefficient` and `exponent`.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.title: Sparse Matrix Representation (Triplet Form)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.simpleConcept: Imagine an attendance sheet with 1,000 students where only 3 students are absent. Instead of printing 1,000 names with 'Present' next to 997 of them, you just write down the 3 roll numbers who are absent. That is a sparse matrix: when most entries are zeros, we only store the non-zero values with their (row, column, value) coordinates.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.technicalConcept:
A sparse matrix is an M x N matrix in which the majority of elements are zero. Storing all elements in a standard 2D array wastes memory (O(M x N)) and CPU cycles processing zeroes.
Triplet Representation (3-Tuple Form):
An array of structures where each element has:
• `row`: Row index of non-zero value
• `col`: Column index of non-zero value
• `val`: Non-zero value
Row 0 (Header/Metadata) stores:
• `triplet[0].row = Total Rows (M)`
• `triplet[0].col = Total Columns (N)`
• `triplet[0].val = Total Non-Zero Elements (K)`
The total space occupied is (K + 1) * 3, dramatically smaller when K << M * N.
keyPoints: A matrix is sparse if zero elements significantly outnumber non-zero elements.
Standard 2D array uses O(rows * cols); Triplet form uses O(non_zeros) storage.
Row 0 is the metadata header storing matrix dimensions and total non-zero count.
Triplets are traditionally sorted by row index, then by column index.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.title: Transposing a Sparse Matrix
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.simpleConcept: Transposing means turning rows into columns (swapping i and j coordinates). If you just swap coordinates naively, the resulting triplet list won't be sorted by rows anymore! An ordinary transpose searches through all columns one by one, which is slow. Fast Transpose uses a frequency count to precalculate the exact destination slot for every element in one smooth pass.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.technicalConcept:
When transposing a sparse triplet representation, swapping `row` and `col` invalidates row-major ordering.
1. Ordinary Transpose: Iterates columns 0 to N-1; scans all K non-zero elements. Time: O(Cols * K).
2. Fast Transpose: Uses `row_terms[]` and `starting_pos[]` to place elements directly into target slots in a single pass. Time: O(Cols + K).
keyPoints: Transposing swaps (row, col) coordinates while preserving sorted row order.
Ordinary Transpose has O(cols * non_zeros) time complexity.
Fast Transpose achieves O(cols + non_zeros) using row_terms[] and starting_pos[] auxiliary arrays.
Fast Transpose requires O(cols) auxiliary memory space.

examModelAnswers.question: Write and explain the Fast Transpose algorithm for sparse matrix representation. Analyze its time complexity.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Concept & Need:
In ordinary transpose, scanning all terms for every column costs O(cols * terms). Fast Transpose uses two auxiliary arrays to achieve O(cols + terms).

2. Auxiliary Arrays:
• `row_terms[col]`: Frequency count of elements in column `col` of matrix A.
• `starting_pos[col]`: Prefix sum starting index in transposed matrix B: `starting_pos[i] = starting_pos[i-1] + row_terms[i-1]` with `starting_pos[0] = 1`.

3. Complexity Analysis:
• Loop 1: O(terms)
• Loop 2: O(cols)
• Loop 3: O(terms)
Total Time Complexity = O(cols + terms), which is linear.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation & Stack Implementations
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.simpleConcept: A stack is like a stack of cafeteria plates: the last plate placed on top is the first one taken off (LIFO: Last-In, First-Out). You can only push a new plate onto the top or pop the top plate off. If the plate dispenser is full, pushing causes an overflow; if it's completely empty, popping causes an underflow.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.technicalConcept:
A Stack is a linear ADT restricted to LIFO (Last-In First-Out) operations occurring exclusively at one end designated as `top`.
• Primary operations:
  - `push(item)`: Increments top and stores item. Fails on Stack Overflow (`top == MAX - 1`).
  - `pop()`: Returns item at top and decrements top. Fails on Stack Underflow (`top == -1`).
  - `peek()`: Inspects top element without removing it.
• Dynamic Implementation: Allocates stack dynamically on the heap; dynamically doubles capacity via `realloc` when full, avoiding static overflow limits.
keyPoints: Stack follows LIFO discipline (Last In, First Out).
Stack Underflow occurs when pop() is attempted on an empty stack (`top == -1`).
Stack Overflow occurs in static arrays when push() is attempted and `top == MAX - 1`.
Dynamic stack uses `realloc` to double buffer size upon overflow, achieving O(1) amortized push.
Crucial in call stacks, undo/redo buffers, syntax parsing, and recursion.

1. Definition:
A Stack is an ordered linear collection where insertion and deletion occur at only one end called `top`, operating on LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle.

2. Operations:
• Push Algorithm:
  Check if `top == MAX - 1`. If yes, output 'Stack Overflow'. Else `top = top + 1; stack[top] = item;`.
• Pop Algorithm:
  Check if `top == -1`. If yes, output 'Stack Underflow'. Else `item = stack[top]; top = top - 1; return item;`.
• Display Algorithm:
  If `top == -1`, stack is empty. Else loop `for (int i = top; i >= 0; i--) print stack[i]`.

3. Time Complexity: Push, Pop, and Peek are all O(1) constant time operations.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion, Postfix Evaluation & Recursion
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.simpleConcept: Humans write expressions in infix notation: `A + B * C`, which requires parentheses and operator rules to know what happens first. Computers hate guessing rules: they prefer postfix (Reverse Polish) notation: `A B C * +`, where operators immediately follow their operands. Stacks convert and evaluate postfix expressions with zero ambiguity and zero parentheses!
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.technicalConcept:
1. Infix to Postfix Conversion (Shunting-Yard):
• Scan infix tokens left to right.
• If operand: output immediately to postfix string.
• If `(`: push to stack.
• If `)`: pop and output until matching `(` is encountered.
• If operator: pop operators with greater or equal precedence from stack to output, then push incoming operator.
• At end of expression: pop all remaining operators.
2. Postfix Evaluation:
• Scan postfix expression left to right.
• If operand: push value onto evaluation stack.
• If operator: pop two operands (`op2 = pop()`, `op1 = pop()`), compute `res = op1 operator op2`, push `res` back onto stack.
• Final answer is the sole value remaining on the stack.
3. Recursion & Run-Time Stack:
• Every recursive function call pushes an activation record (stack frame) storing local variables, parameters, and return address onto the system call stack.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.title: Circular Queues, Double-Ended Queues & Priority Queues
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.simpleConcept: A linear queue is like a movie ticket line: people join at the back (rear) and leave from the front (front). But in a linear array queue, once people leave the front, those empty spots can never be reused without shifting everyone! A Circular Queue bends the line into a circle like a merry-go-round, wrapping around back to slot 0 so space is never wasted.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.technicalConcept:
1. Linear Queue Limitation: False Overflow occurs when `rear == MAX - 1` even though empty slots exist before `front`.
2. Circular Queue:
• Uses modulo arithmetic: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX`, `front = (front + 1) % MAX`.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
• Empty Condition: `front == -1 && rear == -1`.
3. Deque (Double-Ended Queue): Allows insertion and deletion at both ends (`insertFront`, `deleteFront`, `insertRear`, `deleteRear`).
4. Priority Queue: Elements are served based on priority rather than arrival time (implemented using sorted arrays or heaps).
keyPoints: Linear queue suffers from false overflow due to unidirectional pointer movement.
Circular queue wraps around using modulo arithmetic: `(index + 1) % MAX`.
Deque allows operations at both ends (Input-restricted and Output-restricted variants exist).
Priority queues dequeue highest-priority items first, crucial for CPU job scheduling.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.title: Singly, Doubly & Circular Linked Lists Operations
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.simpleConcept: Think of a treasure hunt: you don't need a single big bus where everyone sits in a row (array). Each clue tells you where the next person is located across town (pointers). A Singly Linked List points only forward; a Doubly Linked List gives you clues forward and backward; a Circular Linked List loops the last clue right back to the first person!
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.technicalConcept:
A Linked List is a linear data collection composed of dynamically allocated nodes connected by pointers.
1. Singly Linked List (SLL):
• Each node has `data` and `next` pointer.
• Traversal is strictly unidirectional; inserting/deleting at head is O(1).
2. Doubly Linked List (DLL):
• Each node has `prev`, `data`, and `next` pointers.
• Supports bidirectional traversal and O(1) node deletion given node reference, at the cost of extra pointer overhead.
3. Circular Linked List (CLL):
• The `next` pointer of the last node points back to the `head` node rather than NULL, eliminating null-pointer checks during cyclic traversal.
keyPoints: Linked lists eliminate fixed capacity constraints and expensive array shifting.
SLL node has 1 pointer (`next`); DLL node has 2 pointers (`prev` and `next`).
Inserting at head: `newNode->next = head; head = newNode;` (O(1)).
Deleting a node in DLL: `node->prev->next = node->next; node->next->prev = node->prev; free(node);`
Circular lists are ideal for round-robin CPU scheduling and playlist repeat loops.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: A family tree starts with a single ancestor (root) branching out into children. In a Binary Search Tree (BST), there is a strict rule: smaller children go to the LEFT branch, and bigger children go to the RIGHT branch. Because of this rule, reading the tree 'Inorder' (Left, Root, Right) automatically prints all numbers in perfectly sorted ascending order!
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
1. Binary Tree: A non-linear hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children (`left` and `right`).
2. Binary Search Tree (BST) Property: For every node X:
• All values in `left_subtree(X) < value(X)`
• All values in `right_subtree(X) > value(X)`
3. Tree Traversals:
• Inorder (L-D-R): Traverse left subtree, visit root, traverse right subtree. Produces sorted order in BST.
• Preorder (D-L-R): Visit root, traverse left, traverse right. Used to serialize/clone trees.
• Postorder (L-R-D): Traverse left, traverse right, visit root. Used for bottom-up cleanup (deleting trees) and postfix expressions.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.title: Threaded Binary Trees & AVL Tree Rotations
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.simpleConcept: In a standard binary tree, almost half of all child pointers are NULL (wasted space!). A Threaded Binary Tree replaces those useless NULL pointers with 'threads' pointing to in-order predecessors and successors, allowing you to walk through the tree without recursion or a stack. An AVL Tree is a self-balancing gymnast: whenever one side gets too heavy, it performs rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL) to stay balanced.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.technicalConcept:
1. Threaded Binary Tree (TBT):
• Utilizes empty NULL leaf pointers to store in-order traversal pointers.
• `rthread = 1` indicates `right` points to Inorder successor; `lthread = 1` indicates `left` points to Inorder predecessor.
• Enables stackless, non-recursive Inorder traversal.
2. AVL Trees (Adelson-Velsky and Landis):
• Self-balancing BST where Balance Factor for every node is $BF = \text{height}(left) - \text{height}(right) \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$.
• When $|BF| > 1$, four rotation schemes restore balance:
  - LL Rotation: Single Right rotation on root
  - RR Rotation: Single Left rotation on root
  - LR Rotation: Left rotation on child, then Right rotation on root
  - RL Rotation: Right rotation on child, then Left rotation on root
• Guarantees strictly $O(\log n)$ worst-case search, insertion, and deletion.
keyPoints: In an N-node binary tree, exactly N + 1 pointers are NULL; TBTs repurpose them as threads.
TBT allows traversal without recursion or explicit runtime stacks.
AVL tree balance factor: BF = Height(Left) - Height(Right); must remain in {-1, 0, 1}.
LL and RR require single rotations; LR and RL require double rotations.
AVL trees strictly maintain O(log n) height, preventing O(n) degenerate skewing.

A Binary Heap is a Complete Binary Tree stored compactly in a contiguous array without pointers:
• Array Mapping: For element at index `i`:

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.simpleConcept: Think of a subway network or airline route map: cities are stations (vertices) and routes connecting them are tracks (edges). Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores outward in concentric ripples like waves in a pond using a Queue (closest stations first). Depth-First Search (DFS) explores one deep tunnel all the way to a dead end before backtracking using a Stack or Recursion.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.technicalConcept:
A Graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of vertices $V$ and edges $E$.
1. Representations:
• Adjacency Matrix: $V \times V$ 2D array where `matrix[u][v] = 1` if edge exists. Space: $O(V^2)$, optimal for dense graphs.
• Adjacency List: Array of linked lists where list `u` contains all neighbors of vertex `u`. Space: $O(V + E)$, optimal for sparse graphs.
2. Graph Traversals:
• Breadth-First Search (BFS):
  - Uses a FIFO Queue.
  - Explores all neighbors at current distance before moving deeper.
  - Time: $O(V + E)$. Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.
• Depth-First Search (DFS):
  - Uses LIFO Stack / Recursion.
  - Traverses as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.
  - Time: $O(V + E)$. Used for cycle detection and topological sorting.
keyPoints: Adjacency Matrix uses O(V^2) space; Adjacency List uses O(V + E) space.
BFS uses a Queue and visits vertices level-by-level (radiating outwards).
DFS uses a Stack / recursion and explores paths to dead ends before backtracking.
Both BFS and DFS maintain a `visited[]` boolean array to prevent infinite cycles.
Traversing an entire graph with BFS or DFS takes O(V + E) using adjacency lists.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.title: Hash Functions & Collision Resolution Techniques
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.simpleConcept: Think of an apartment building with mailboxes numbered 0 to 99. A hash function takes your name and calculates which mailbox slot your letter belongs to in one second (O(1)). But what if two people get assigned the exact same mailbox? That is a Collision! We resolve it either by chaining (hanging a bag underneath the mailbox) or linear probing (placing it into the next available open mailbox).
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.technicalConcept:
Hashing maps a large key space to a compact hash table index using a Hash Function $h(k)$.
1. Common Hash Functions:
• Division Method: $h(k) = k \pmod m$ (where $m$ is usually a prime number).
• Multiplication Method: $h(k) = \lfloor m (k A \pmod 1) \rfloor$.
• Mid-Square Method: Square the key and extract middle digits.
2. Collision Resolution Techniques:
• Open Hashing (Separate Chaining):
  - Each hash table slot is the head of a linked list storing all colliding keys.
  - Table never fills up; degrades gracefully as load factor $\alpha = n/m$ increases.
• Closed Hashing (Open Addressing):
  - All keys stored directly in table slots.
  - Linear Probing: $h(k, i) = (h(k) + i) \pmod m$. Suffers from primary clustering.
  - Quadratic Probing: $h(k, i) = (h(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) \pmod m$. Reduces clustering.
  - Double Hashing: $h(k, i) = (h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \pmod m$. Optimal dispersion.
keyPoints: Hashing achieves O(1) average-case search, insertion, and deletion.

Linear Probing checks consecutive slots, causing primary clustering clusters of filled slots.
Load factor alpha = n / m measures table saturation.

vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t1.title: Hash Functions & Collision Resolution Techniques
vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t1.simpleConcept: Think of an apartment building with mailboxes numbered 0 to 99. A hash function takes your name and calculates which mailbox slot your letter belongs to in one second (O(1)). But what if two people get assigned the exact same mailbox? That is a Collision! We resolve it either by chaining (hanging a bag underneath the mailbox) or linear probing (placing it into the next available open mailbox).
vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t1.technicalConcept:
Hashing maps a large key space to a compact hash table index using a Hash Function $h(k)$.
1. Common Hash Functions:
• Division Method: $h(k) = k \pmod m$ (where $m$ is usually a prime number).
• Multiplication Method: $h(k) = \lfloor m (k A \pmod 1) \rfloor$.
• Mid-Square Method: Square the key and extract middle digits.
2. Collision Resolution Techniques:
• Open Hashing (Separate Chaining):
  - Each hash table slot is the head of a linked list storing all colliding keys.
  - Table never fills up; degrades gracefully as load factor $\alpha = n/m$ increases.
• Closed Hashing (Open Addressing):
  - All keys stored directly in table slots.
  - Linear Probing: $h(k, i) = (h(k) + i) \pmod m$. Suffers from primary clustering.
  - Quadratic Probing: $h(k, i) = (h(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) \pmod m$. Reduces clustering.
  - Double Hashing: $h(k, i) = (h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \pmod m$. Optimal dispersion.
keyPoints: Hashing achieves O(1) average-case search, insertion, and deletion.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.title: Merge Sort, Quick Sort & Radix Sort Complexity Analysis
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.simpleConcept: Sorting organizes messy books by title. Merge Sort is like a wise librarian who divides a giant stack into two equal halves, sorts each half, and merges them smoothly (guaranteed fast). Quick Sort picks a leader ('pivot') and tosses smaller books to the left and bigger books to the right. Radix Sort doesn't compare books at all: it sorts numbers digit by digit like postal mail sorting machines!
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.technicalConcept:
1. Merge Sort:
• Divide-and-Conquer paradigm.
• Divides array into halves, recursively sorts, and merges two sorted halves in $O(n)$ time.
• Recurrence: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) \implies O(n \log n)$ across all cases (best, average, worst).
• Stable sort, but requires $O(n)$ auxiliary space.
2. Quick Sort:
• Selects pivot element, partitions array into elements $\le$ pivot and $>$ pivot.
• Average Case: $O(n \log n)$. Worst Case: $O(n^2)$ when array is already sorted and pivot is extreme.
• In-place sort requiring $O(\log n)$ stack space.
3. Radix Sort:
• Non-comparative integer sorting algorithm.
• Processes digits from Least Significant Digit (LSD) to MSD using stable Counting Sort subroutines.
• Time Complexity: $O(d \cdot (n + k))$ where $d$ is maximum digits, $k$ is base/radix (10 for decimal).
keyPoints: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases, but requires O(n) auxiliary memory.
Quick Sort has O(n log n) average time and O(n^2) worst case, but operates in-place.
Quick Sort worst case is mitigated by randomized or median-of-three pivot selection.
Radix Sort is non-comparative, beating the O(n log n) comparison barrier with O(d * (n + k)).
Merge Sort and Radix Sort are Stable; standard Quick Sort is Unstable.

examModelAnswers.question: Write the algorithm for Quick Sort and trace it for the array [26, 5, 37, 1, 61, 11, 59, 15]. Discuss its worst-case complexity.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Quick Sort Algorithm:
1. Choose a pivot element (e.g. first element `arr[low]`).
2. Partition array using two pointers `i` and `j` such that elements < pivot are left and elements > pivot are right.
3. Swap pivot into its correct sorted position `j`.
4. Recursively call `quickSort(arr, low, j - 1)` and `quickSort(arr, j + 1, high)`.

2. Partition Trace of [26, 5, 37, 1, 61, 11, 59, 15]:
• Pivot = 26.
• Left scans forward for element > 26 (finds 37).
• Right scans backward for element < 26 (finds 15).
• Swap 37 and 15 -> [26, 5, 15, 1, 61, 11, 59, 37].
• Continue: swap 61 and 11 -> [26, 5, 15, 1, 11, 61, 59, 37].
• Pointers cross at index 4 (value 11). Swap pivot 26 with 11:
• Partitioned array: [11, 5, 15, 1] 26 [61, 59, 37]. Pivot 26 is placed.

3. Worst-Case Complexity Analysis:
Occurs when array is already sorted or reverse sorted and extreme element is always chosen as pivot.
Recurrence: T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(n) = O(n^2). Avoided via randomized or median-of-three pivot.
